notes.meaning: Paul tells the church in Rome to welcome believers whose faith is still tender and full of worries. These Christians had extra rules about what was allowed, but they were still genuine brothers and sisters. Stronger Christians should receive them warmly into church fellowship without arguing over their personal opinions.

One believer understands that Christian freedom allows eating any kind of food. Another believer worries that meat sold in the city might be unclean or offered to idols, so they eat only vegetables to stay safe. Both people are trying to follow God, but they see the rules differently.

The person who feels free to eat meat must not look down on the person who abstains as being narrow-minded. At the same time, the one who abstains must not condemn the meat-eater as sinful or careless. God has welcomed both into His family through Christ, so believers must welcome each other too.

Paul asks what right anyone has to judge a servant who belongs to someone else. Every believer belongs directly to Jesus, and only Jesus has the authority to decide if their life pleases Him. The Lord has the power to keep His followers standing secure in the faith despite their differences.

Some believers felt that certain Jewish festival days still had to be observed as holy. Other believers treated every day as belonging to God in the same way under the new covenant. Rather than copying others blindly, each Christian needs to think carefully and follow what they are convinced is right before God.

differ.view: Methodist teachers traditionally hold that Paul is discussing only Jewish ceremonial feast days, not the weekly Sabbath or the Christian Lord's Day.
Anglican commentators often explain that observing sacred days has no absolute divine command under the gospel, but churches may appoint them for spiritual order and benefit.

notes.meaning: Both groups act out of a sincere desire to honor God. The one who eats meat gives thanks at meals, and the one who eats only plants gives thanks for what God provides. What matters most to God is that the believer's heart is set on pleasing and thanking Him.

Christians do not belong to themselves or live just to please their own wishes. In both life and death, believers belong wholly to Jesus and aim to bring Him honor. Because Christ is our true Master, every part of our daily life is placed under His care and guidance.

Jesus died and returned to life so that He would have rightful rule over all His people forever. His authority reaches over believers who have passed away and those who are still alive. Since He bought us with His life, He is the only Judge we must answer to.

Paul challenges both groups in the church to examine their attitudes. The scrupulous believer must not condemn their fellow Christian, and the confident believer must not despise their brother or sister. God will place every believer before His own throne of judgment, so no human being should take God's place as judge.

Paul quotes the prophet Isaiah to show that every person must bow before God and acknowledge His supreme rule. In the end, each Christian will answer directly to God for their own choices and conduct. We will not be called to give an account of our neighbor's minor opinions, only our own lives.

Believers should give up the habit of criticizing and condemning one another. Instead, they should use their judgment to make sure their own actions do not trip up a fellow believer. A stumbling block means anything that tempts another person to sin or damages their walk with God.

Paul agrees with the stronger believers that no food is dirty or sinful in its own nature under the new covenant. Yet if a person genuinely believes in their conscience that eating a certain food is wrong, doing so would be a sin for them. Conscience must be respected even when a person is still learning the full freedom of the gospel.

If eating a certain food hurts another believer or tempts them to violate their conscience, that action is unloving. Christ loved that person enough to lay down His life for them on the cross. Giving up a plate of food is a very small sacrifice compared to the price Jesus paid to save them.

differ.view: Methodist interpreters understand 'destroy' to show that a real believer for whom Christ died can fall into sin and ultimately be lost.
Reformed interpreters teach that this warning describes the dangerous tendency of leading a brother into sin, though God's elect are ultimately preserved from final ruin.

notes.meaning: Christian freedom is a good gift from God, but it can easily be misunderstood. If believers use their liberty selfishly and cause arguments or hurt others, people outside the faith will speak ill of the church and the gospel. Believers must handle their freedom wisely so that Christ's truth is honored.

True faith is not defined by outward rules about food or drink. God's kingdom is centered on living right before God, living in peace with others, and experiencing true spiritual joy through the Holy Spirit. These spiritual blessings matter far more than insisting on our personal rights.

Anyone who serves Jesus by focusing on righteousness, peace, and joy pleases the Lord. Good people in the world also respect a life marked by this kind of genuine uprightness and harmony. Living this way shows the beauty of Christ far better than arguing over food.

Believers should actively chase after things that bring peace among church members. To edify means to build up someone else in their spiritual life and understanding. Christians should spend their energy helping one another grow strong rather than tearing each other down with arguments.

God is doing a precious work of building faith and love in each Christian's life. It is foolish to tear down that spiritual building just to eat whatever food we want. All foods are clean to eat, but eating becomes sinful when it causes another person to trip and fall into sin.

Paul urges believers to willingly set aside their privileges, such as eating meat or drinking wine, if it helps protect a brother's walk with God. Love for others is always more important than personal rights. True Christian maturity means choosing self-denial so that others can stay strong in the faith.

If you understand your Christian liberty before God, you do not need to show it off in public to prove a point. Enjoy that freedom quietly in your personal relationship with God. Happy is the believer who can enjoy their freedom without feeling guilty in their own conscience or hurting someone else.

A person who eats while still doubting whether God allows it stands guilty, because they are acting against their conscience. Whenever someone does something without being convinced that it pleases God, they are choosing to risk disobeying Him. Christians must always act out of clear confidence and trust in the Lord.

differ.view: Reformed teachers often apply this broadly to mean that any action not done out of faith in God, including the good deeds of unbelievers, is sinful.
Methodist teachers understand this specifically within the context, meaning that whatever a person does while doubting its lawfulness becomes sin to them.
